title: Message Queues
oneLiner: Put a buffer between the service that produces work and the one that does it, and plan for every message arriving twice.
keyTakeaway: A queue decouples producers from consumers and absorbs bursts, so a spike becomes a backlog instead of an outage. Real queues deliver at least once, which means duplicates will happen: make consumers idempotent (processing the same message twice has the same effect as once) and send messages that keep failing to a dead-letter queue.
explanation:
A message queue sits between a producer (the service that creates work, like the checkout service saying "order 1001 was placed") and consumers (the services that do the work, like charging the card or sending the email). The producer puts a message on the queue and moves on; it doesn't need to know who reads it, how many consumers there are, or whether they are up right now. SQS, RabbitMQ and Kafka are the names you will hear.

The first thing a queue buys you is smoothing. Press the traffic spike button: for 3 seconds producers publish 10 times faster than the consumers can work. Without a queue those requests would time out or overload the downstream service. With one, the extra messages wait, the oldest message gets older for a while, and then the backlog drains. But a queue only smooths bursts. If producers are faster than consumers on average, the queue grows without limit, and the fix is more consumers or back-pressure: making producers slow down, rejecting work, or capping the queue size so the problem shows up at the edge instead of hours later.

Delivery guarantees come in three flavors. At-most-once means a message is removed before it is processed, so a crash loses it. At-least-once means it is removed only after the consumer acknowledges it; if the consumer crashes before the ack, the message becomes visible again after a visibility timeout and someone else processes it. That's what the crash button shows, and it is what most real systems do. Delivery between two separate systems can't do better than at-least-once: when an ack is lost, the sender can't tell whether the message arrived, so it must send again.

"Exactly once" is a claim about processing, not delivery, and it holds within a bounded scope. Inside Kafka, for example, a transaction commits the consumed offsets and the produced records atomically, so a step that reads from one topic and writes to another takes effect once. Any other side effect needs an idempotent consumer: it stores each message id it has processed in the same database transaction as its own local effect (an order row, a ledger entry) and skips ids it has already seen.

Charging a card doesn't fit that pattern, because the card processor is another company's system and can't join your database transaction. If the consumer charges the card and crashes before recording the message id, the redelivered message charges again. The fix is the processor's own idempotency key: send one derived from the order, the same on every retry, and the processor returns the original result instead of charging twice. Then reconcile: regularly compare your records with the processor's to catch anything that slipped through, such as a charge whose response was lost. Idempotency Keys and Safe Retries covers the same pattern from the API side. Without any of this, the customer gets charged twice.

A poison message is one that fails every time, for example malformed data. If it is retried forever it wastes a consumer on every attempt and, in an ordered queue, blocks everything behind it. The standard answer is a retry limit (3 here) and a dead-letter queue where failed messages are parked for a human or a repair job.

Ordering is the other big topic. A single queue with many consumers does not preserve order: two messages can be processed at the same time and finish in either order. Kafka-style logs split a topic into partitions, each of which is strictly ordered and read by one consumer in a group at a time. You pick a partition key, such as the order id or user id, so all messages for the same order land in the same partition and stay in order, while different orders are processed in parallel. The number of partitions caps how many consumers can work in parallel.

Use a direct call when the caller needs the answer right now to continue, like checking a password or reading a price. Use a queue when the work can happen a little later, when the downstream service is slower or less reliable than the caller, when traffic is bursty, or when several services need to react to the same event. The cost is that the system becomes eventually consistent (parts of it catch up a little later rather than instantly) and harder to trace, so a queue is a decision, not a default.
